query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA (such as CoCrFeMnNi), high-rate deformation or service at moderately elevated temperatures initiates a transition in the grain-boundary structure whereby dynamic grain refinement (even in the absence of classical impurity segregation) promotes nanoclustering of principal elements at the boundaries. This clustering reduces the local cohesive energy, triggering cavitation and premature fracture along grain boundaries and triple junctions, thereby causing a loss of toughness and the emergence of brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A coarse-grained, single-phase HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) with a uniformly disordered solid solution and no significant grain-boundary segregation or deleterious precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled mechanical deformation (e.g., tensile or sliding contact tests) under high strain-rate conditions in an ultra-high vacuum environment to eliminate oxidation effects, while also including a quasi-static deformation control.
generation.conditions: Tests performed across room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures (up to about 400°C) under inert (UHV) conditions and at varying strain rates (high versus low) to provoke dynamic microstructural changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the grain-boundary structure into an ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically refined layer with localized nanoclustering of elements (notably Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain-rate or elevated temperature loading, intense shear leads to dynamic amorphization and grain refinement. The loss of dislocation‐mediated plasticity in these ultrafine regions, together with the spontaneous nanoclustering of principal elements at the refined grain boundaries, lowers the interfacial cohesive energy, thereby facilitating cavitation and brittle decohesion along the interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained state, deformed samples under high strain rates should exhibit an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer with measurable nanoporosity at grain boundaries, accompanied by reduced toughness and an earlier onset of brittle failure. In contrast, under quasi-static conditions, the microstructure and toughness should remain closer to the initial ductile baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial, coarse-grained, single-phase HEA exhibiting high toughness and ductility when deformed under low strain-rate or steady-state conditions in an inert environment.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to prevail under service conditions where high strain rates or moderate temperature exposure promote dynamic grain boundary evolution; outside this regime (e.g., at very low strain rates or in oxidizing environments), different failure mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical strain rate and temperature thresholds that trigger significant dynamic grain refinement and nanoclustering remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples. Deform one set under high strain-rate conditions in ultra-high vacuum (UHV) and a second set under quasi-static conditions as a control. After deformation, characterize the microstructure via TEM/STEM and atom probe tomography to assess grain size and element clustering at the boundaries. Perform fracture toughness and tensile tests to evaluate mechanical performance.
measurements: Grain size distribution (particularly near the surface) using TEM/STEM
Detection of nanoclustering or changes in compositional homogeneity at grain boundaries via atom probe tomography
Fracture toughness and ductility from mechanical testing
Observation of cavitation or microcrack initiation at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain-rate deformed samples do not exhibit a significant grain refinement accompanied by detectable nanoclustering at grain boundaries, and if the mechanical tests reveal no significant reduction in toughness (i.e. the failure remains ductile and similar to the quasi-static control), then the hypothesis that dynamic grain-boundary decohesion via nanoclustering drives brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
